summary: Moses expresses doubt about his ability to lead the Israelites, so God gives him three miraculous signs to perform and appoints his brother Aaron as his spokesperson. Moses then prepares to return to Egypt with his family, receiving a warning from God about Pharaoh's hardened heart and a threat against Pharaoh's firstborn. On the journey, God confronts Moses, and his wife Zipporah performs a circumcision to avert danger. Finally, Moses and Aaron meet, gather the Israelite elders, perform the signs, and the people believe.
setting: This chapter is set in Midian, where Moses has been living, and then on the journey back to Egypt, and finally in Egypt itself. Moses is returning to lead the Israelites out of slavery, a task he was given by God in the previous chapter.

events.what: Moses tells God he fears the Israelites will not believe him or that God has appeared to him.

God instructs Moses to throw his staff down, which turns into a snake. Moses flees, but God tells him to pick it up by the tail, and it turns back into a staff. This is given as a sign for the Israelites to believe.
God tells Moses to put his hand into his cloak, and when he takes it out, it is leprous. God then tells him to put it back in, and it becomes healthy again. This is a second sign for the Israelites.
God promises a third sign: if the people do not believe the first two, Moses can take water from the Nile, pour it on the ground, and it will turn into blood.
Moses protests again, claiming he is not eloquent and is slow of speech and tongue.
God responds by asserting his power over human speech and promises to be with Moses' mouth and teach him what to say.
Moses asks God to send someone else instead.

God becomes angry and appoints Aaron, Moses' brother, as Moses' spokesperson. God says Aaron will speak to the people for Moses, and Moses will be like God to Aaron, and Moses will still use the staff for signs.

Moses gets permission from his father-in-law Jethro to return to Egypt. God tells Moses that those who sought his life in Egypt are dead. Moses takes his wife and sons and the 'staff of God' and begins the journey back to Egypt.

God tells Moses that he will harden Pharaoh's heart so Pharaoh will not let the Israelites go. God instructs Moses to tell Pharaoh that Israel is God's firstborn son, and if Pharaoh refuses to let them go, God will kill Pharaoh's firstborn son.

At a lodging place, God confronts Moses and seeks to kill him. Moses' wife Zipporah quickly circumcises their son with a sharp stone, touches Moses' feet with the foreskin, and says, 'You are a bridegroom of blood to me.' God then leaves Moses.

God tells Aaron to meet Moses in the wilderness. They meet at the mountain of God, and Moses tells Aaron all God's instructions and signs. Moses and Aaron then gather the elders of Israel, Aaron speaks to them, performs the signs, and the people believe, bowing down and worshipping.

people.name: Moses
people.role: Chosen by God to lead the Israelites, but expresses doubt and reluctance.

people.name: Jehovah
people.role: The God who commissions Moses, gives him signs, and directs his actions.

people.name: Aaron
people.role: Moses' brother, appointed by God to be Moses' spokesperson to the people and Pharaoh.

people.name: Jethro
people.role: Moses' father-in-law, who grants Moses permission to return to Egypt.

people.name: Zipporah
people.role: Moses' wife, who performs a circumcision to save Moses' life.

people.name: Moses' sons
people.role: Travel with Moses and Zipporah; one of them is circumcised by Zipporah.

people.name: Pharaoh
people.role: The king of Egypt, whose heart God says he will harden.

people.name: Israelites
people.role: The people whom Moses is sent to deliver; they believe God's message and signs.

people.name: Elders of Israel
people.role: Leaders of the Israelite people who are gathered by Moses and Aaron.

terms.meaning: A severe skin condition that, in ancient times, was often associated with ritual impurity and could involve white, scaly patches (v. 6).
A wooden rod carried by Moses, which God empowers to perform miraculous signs (v. 20).
A phrase describing God's action to make Pharaoh resistant to Moses' demands, preventing him from letting the Israelites leave (v. 21).
A place where travelers would stop to rest or stay overnight during a journey (v. 24).
The cutting off of the foreskin, a ritual practice that served as a sign of the covenant between God and Abraham's descendants (v. 25).
A phrase spoken by Zipporah after circumcising her son, likely referring to the covenant sealed by blood, or perhaps a protective act related to the shedding of blood (v. 25).

readings.view: This chapter is often read as highlighting Moses' profound humility and initial reluctance to accept his divine mission (vv. 10-13). The incident at the lodging place (vv. 24-26) is seen as a critical reminder of the absolute necessity of fulfilling the covenant of circumcision, even for a prophet like Moses, and the danger of neglecting divine commands.

Many Christian readings emphasize God's ability to equip those he calls, despite their perceived weaknesses, as seen in Moses' speech impediment and God's provision of Aaron (vv. 10-16). The hardening of Pharaoh's heart (v. 21) and the threat against his firstborn (v. 23) are often seen as foreshadowing God's ultimate judgment and power over human rulers.

Scholars often note the abruptness and unusual nature of the divine attack on Moses (vv. 24-26), suggesting it may be an ancient, independent narrative fragment that was later incorporated into the larger Exodus story. They also examine the tension between God hardening Pharaoh's heart (v. 21) and the idea of human free will, often exploring how these concepts function within the narrative's theological framework.

oftenQuoted.caution: This verse, 'Who makes a person's mouth? Who makes the mute, or the deaf, or the seeing, or the blind? Is it not I, Jehovah?', is often quoted to assert God's sovereignty over human abilities and disabilities. In its context, it is God's direct response to Moses' claim of being a poor speaker, assuring Moses that God, who created speech, will enable him to speak for the mission.

The phrase 'I will harden his heart' is frequently quoted in discussions about divine sovereignty and human free will. Within the chapter, it is God's declaration to Moses that Pharaoh will resist the demand to let Israel go, despite the signs, indicating that God's plan involves Pharaoh's resistance leading to further divine action.
